Every part of this lab follows the same five steps: state the decision, look at the data, name the assumption,
compute in R and write one sentence for the person who has to act. All numbers are *synthetic* or teaching
*assumptions*; none describes a commercial product or a real emergency department.

If R is new to you, read the code and the printed output first and answer the questions on paper; the printed
results are complete. If you are fluent in R, try the extra counter-check at the end of each part.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

```

## Part A · The same alert in two referral settings (unit 09) {#part-a}

**Decision.** A fictitious emergency department considers a tool that suggests a second look at a wrist
radiograph when it flags a possible fracture. Clinicians want to know how many alerts per shift will turn out to
be fractures.

**Assumption.** In both settings the tool has a sensitivity and a specificity of 90% (*assumption*). In the first
setting 5 of 100 people examined have a fracture, in the second 20 of 100. Whether the tool really reaches 90% in
either setting is *open* and would need a local study.

Before you run the code, cover the right-hand columns of the printed table and fill in a two-by-two table for
1,000 examinations by hand. Who belongs in the denominator of the positive predictive value?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Part A (unit 09): 1,000 examinations in each of two referral settings
scenarios <- data.frame(
  setting     = c("Low prevalence (5%)", "Higher prevalence (20%)"),
  n           = c(1000, 1000),
  prevalence  = c(0.05, 0.20),
  sensitivity = c(0.90, 0.90),   # assumption, identical in both settings
  specificity = c(0.90, 0.90)    # assumption, identical in both settings
)
scenarios$fracture    <- scenarios$n * scenarios$prevalence
scenarios$no_fracture <- scenarios$n - scenarios$fracture
scenarios$tp <- scenarios$sensitivity * scenarios$fracture       # true alerts
scenarios$fn <- scenarios$fracture - scenarios$tp                # missed fractures
scenarios$tn <- scenarios$specificity * scenarios$no_fracture    # correct all-clear
scenarios$fp <- scenarios$no_fracture - scenarios$tn             # false alerts
scenarios$alerts <- scenarios$tp + scenarios$fp
scenarios$ppv <- scenarios$tp / scenarios$alerts                 # share of alerts that are fractures
scenarios$npv <- scenarios$tn / (scenarios$tn + scenarios$fn)    # share of all-clears without fracture
print(scenarios[, c("setting", "tp", "fp", "fn", "tn", "alerts", "ppv", "npv")], digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                   setting  tp fp fn  tn alerts   ppv   npv
#> 1     Low prevalence (5%)  45 95  5 855    140 0.321 0.994
#> 2 Higher prevalence (20%) 180 80 20 720    260 0.692 0.973
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}

  isTRUE(all.equal(scenarios$fp, c(95, 80))),
  isTRUE(all.equal(scenarios$fn, c(5, 20))),
  isTRUE(all.equal(scenarios$tn, c(855, 720))),
  isTRUE(all.equal(scenarios$alerts, c(140, 260))),

)
```
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
  type    = factor(rep(c("Fracture present (true alert)", "No fracture (false alert)"), each = 2),

)
```

**Report.** In the low-prevalence setting, 45 of 140 alerts concern a fracture
(PPV 32.1%); in the higher-prevalence setting it is 180 of
260 (69.2%). A defensible handover sentence for the first setting
reads: *"In our teaching scenario about one in three alerts was a fracture; the image is re-read in its clinical
context."* The lower PPV alone is no reason to reject a tool. Whether the second look improves treatment is a
different question that needs a comparison group and patient-relevant outcomes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Counter-check: predict first"}
Specificity improves from 90% to 95% in the low-prevalence setting, sensitivity stays at 90%. Will the PPV rise to
about 40%, 50% or 60%? Write down your guess, then run the chunk.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Counter-check: predict first, then compute. Specificity rises from 90% to 95% at 5% prevalence.
fp_new  <- (1 - 0.95) * 950
ppv_new <- 45 / (45 + fp_new)
cat("False alerts:", fp_new, " PPV:", cdsr_percent(ppv_new), "\n")
```

## Part B · A baseline and an alternative on the same test patients (unit 10) {#part-b}

**Decision.** The team wants to know whether a more complex model ranks patients better than a simple logistic
regression with four predictors chosen in advance. Both are judged on the same, fixed test patients.

**Look at the data.** The synthetic cohort has 2,000 admissions with suspected wrist fracture. The reference
standard (fracture yes or no) is known for everyone. 600 admissions are drawn once as the test set; their
identifiers are stored with the data, so another group can reproduce exactly the same split.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Part B (unit 10): synthetic emergency department admissions with suspected wrist fracture
set.seed(20260309)
n <- 2000
cohort <- data.frame(id = sprintf("ED%04d", seq_len(n)))
cohort$age <- round(runif(n, 18, 95))                                  # years
cohort$age_group <- factor(ifelse(cohort$age >= 75, "75 and older", "18 to 74"),
                           levels = c("18 to 74", "75 and older"))
cohort$fall_outstretched <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.55)                         # fall on outstretched hand (0/1)
# Reference standard (fracture yes/no) depends on age and mechanism
lp <- -2.6 + 0.02 * (cohort$age - 50) + 1.0 * cohort$fall_outstretched
cohort$fracture <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp))
# Clinical signs: in older patients both signs are weaker indicators (synthetic assumption)
older <- cohort$age_group == "75 and older"
cohort$snuffbox_tender <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(cohort$fracture == 1, ifelse(older, 0.55, 0.80), 0.25))
cohort$swelling        <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(cohort$fracture == 1, ifelse(older, 0.45, 0.80), 0.20))
cohort$grip_kg <- round(rnorm(n, 32 - 0.15 * (cohort$age - 50) - 5 * cohort$fracture, 6), 1)
cohort$grip_kg[sample(n, 100)] <- NA                                   # 5% not measured
cohort$noise <- round(rnorm(n), 2)                                     # unrelated variable

# Fixed test set: 600 admissions drawn once and stored with the data
test_ids <- sort(sample(cohort$id, 600))
cohort$split <- ifelse(cohort$id %in% test_ids, "test", "train")
train <- cohort[cohort$split == "train", ]
test  <- cohort[cohort$split == "test", ]
stopifnot(nrow(train) == 1400, nrow(test) == 600,
          length(intersect(train$id, test$id)) == 0)
table(split = cohort$split, fracture = cohort$fracture)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>        fracture
#> split      0    1
#>   test   516   84
#>   train 1180  220
```


:::
:::


**Assumption.** Grip strength is missing for 5% of admissions. Any pre-processing step, here the median used to
fill in missing grip strength, is learnt from the training data only and then applied unchanged to the test set.
Using the median of all 2,000 admissions would leak information from the test set into the model.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Pre-processing uses training data only: the training median replaces missing grip strength
grip_median_train <- median(train$grip_kg, na.rm = TRUE)
impute_grip <- function(d) {
  d$grip_missing <- as.integer(is.na(d$grip_kg))
  d$grip_kg[is.na(d$grip_kg)] <- grip_median_train
  d
}
train <- impute_grip(train)
test  <- impute_grip(test)
grip_median_train
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 30.3
```


:::
:::


The alternative model is an elastic net with all variables and all pairwise interactions. Its penalty is tuned by
five-fold cross-validation **inside the training data**; the test set is touched once, at the end.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Null model: everyone receives the training prevalence
p_null <- mean(train$fracture)
# Baseline: logistic regression with four pre-specified predictors
baseline <- glm(fracture ~ age + fall_outstretched + snuffbox_tender + swelling,
                family = binomial, data = train)
# Alternative: elastic net with all variables and their pairwise interactions;
# the penalty is tuned by 5-fold cross-validation inside the training data only
f_alt <- ~ (age + fall_outstretched + snuffbox_tender + swelling + grip_kg + grip_missing + noise)^2
x_train <- model.matrix(f_alt, train)[, -1]
x_test  <- model.matrix(f_alt, test)[, -1]
fold_id <- rep_len(1:5, nrow(train))[order(train$id)]      # fixed, reproducible folds
alt_fit <- cv.glmnet(x_train, train$fracture, family = "binomial", alpha = 0.5, foldid = fold_id)

test$p_null     <- p_null
test$p_baseline <- predict(baseline, newdata = test, type = "response")
test$p_alt      <- as.numeric(predict(alt_fit, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "response"))

# Performance on the fixed test set
brier <- function(p, y) mean((p - y)^2)
calib <- function(p, y) {                       # calibration intercept and slope
  lp <- qlogis(pmin(pmax(p, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6))
  c(intercept = unname(coef(glm(y ~ offset(lp), family = binomial))[1]),
    slope = unname(coef(glm(y ~ lp, family = binomial))[2]))
}
results <- data.frame(
  model = c("Null model (training prevalence)", "Baseline: logistic regression, 4 predictors",
            "Alternative: elastic net with interactions"),
  n_test = nrow(test), fractures_test = sum(test$fracture),
  auc   = c(0.5, auc_rank(test$p_baseline, test$fracture), auc_rank(test$p_alt, test$fracture)),
  brier = c(brier(test$p_null, test$fracture), brier(test$p_baseline, test$fracture),
            brier(test$p_alt, test$fracture)),
  calib_slope = c(NA, calib(test$p_baseline, test$fracture)["slope"],
                  calib(test$p_alt, test$fracture)["slope"])
)
print(results, digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                                         model n_test fractures_test   auc
#> 1            Null model (training prevalence)    600             84 0.500
#> 2 Baseline: logistic regression, 4 predictors    600             84 0.858
#> 3  Alternative: elastic net with interactions    600             84 0.883
#>    brier calib_slope
#> 1 0.1207          NA
#> 2 0.0907        0.86
#> 3 0.0803        1.18
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}

  results$n_test[1] == 600,
  all(results$auc[2:3] > 0.65 & results$auc[2:3] < 0.95),
  all(results$brier[2:3] < results$brier[1]),       # both models beat the null model
  abs(results$auc[3] - results$auc[2]) < 0.05        # small gain in ranking for considerably more effort
)
```

**Report.** On the same 600 test admissions, the baseline reaches an AUC of
0.858 and the elastic net 0.883. The difference in
ranking is small compared with the additional effort for tuning, documentation and maintenance; whether it matters
depends on the decision the score is meant to support, which Part C makes concrete.

## Part C · Calibration, threshold and who carries the errors (unit 11) {#part-c}

**Decision.** At which predicted risk should the tool raise an alert, and which group pays for that choice in missed
fractures or unnecessary extra imaging?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Part C (unit 11): calibration by fifths of predicted risk in the test set
calib_bins <- function(p, y, model) {
  bin <- cut(p, quantile(p, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2)), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(data.frame(p, y), bin), function(d) {
    ci <- prop_ci(sum(d$y), nrow(d))
    data.frame(model = model, predicted = mean(d$p), observed = ci[["estimate"]],
               lower = ci[["lower"]], upper = ci[["upper"]], n = nrow(d))
  }))
}
calib_df <- rbind(calib_bins(test$p_baseline, test$fracture, "Baseline"),
                  calib_bins(test$p_alt, test$fracture, "Elastic net"))
p_calib <- ggplot(calib_df, aes(predicted, observed, colour = model, shape = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "22", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = model)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "orange")])) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cdsr_shapes[1:2]) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = cdsr_linetypes[1:2]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted risk in the group", y = "Observed share with fracture (95% CI)",
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       caption = "Synthetic test set, n = 600 admissions in five groups of 120 per model; dashed line = perfect calibration.") +
  theme_cdsr()
show_figure(p_calib, "w3-calibration.png")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Calibration of both models in the synthetic test set: mean predicted risk against the observed share of fractures in five groups of equal size per model, with exact 95% confidence intervals. n = 600 admissions.](lab-w3-diagnostic-accuracy_files/figure-html/fig-w3-calibration-1.png){#fig-w3-calibration fig-alt='Calibration plot. Both models follow the diagonal for low predicted risks. In the highest risk group the baseline predicts about 56% but observes about 45%, so it overestimates risk there; the elastic net lies close to the diagonal. Confidence intervals are wide, about plus or minus 9 percentage points in the top group.' width=1050}
:::
:::


A good AUC says that patients with fractures tend to receive higher scores. It does not say that a predicted risk of
50% means that half of these patients have a fracture. The calibration plot answers that second question.

Now move the threshold. The shift size of 30 wrist examinations is an *assumption* used to translate rates into a
workload that clinicians recognise.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Moving the threshold for the baseline model; 30 wrist examinations per shift (assumption)
per_shift <- 30
threshold_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40), function(t) {
  alert <- test$p_baseline >= t
  y <- test$fracture == 1
  data.frame(threshold = t, alerts = sum(alert), tp = sum(alert & y), fp = sum(alert & !y),
             fn = sum(!alert & y), sensitivity = mean(alert[y]), specificity = mean(!alert[!y]),
             ppv = sum(alert & y) / sum(alert),
             false_alerts_per_shift = per_shift * sum(alert & !y) / nrow(test))
}))
print(threshold_table, digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#> 2       0.2    163 60 103 24       0.714       0.800 0.368
#> 3       0.3    124 54  70 30       0.643       0.864 0.435
#> 4       0.4     92 47  45 37       0.560       0.913 0.511
```

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(all(diff(threshold_table$alerts) <= 0),        # higher threshold, fewer alerts
          all(diff(threshold_table$sensitivity) <= 0))   # ... and fewer fractures detected
```
:::


Finally, look at errors by age group at an example threshold of 20%. Every rate is given with its denominator and
an exact 95% confidence interval.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Errors by age group at the example threshold of 20%, with denominators and exact 95% intervals
threshold <- 0.20
test$alert <- test$p_baseline >= threshold
subgroup_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(test, test$age_group), function(d) {
  y <- d$fracture == 1
  data.frame(age_group = d$age_group[1], admissions = nrow(d), fractures = sum(y),
             detected = format_prop(sum(d$alert & y), sum(y)),
             missed = sum(!d$alert & y),
             false_alerts = format_prop(sum(d$alert & !y), sum(!y)))
}))
print(subgroup_table, row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     age_group admissions fractures                       detected missed
#>      18 to 74        431        46 35/46 = 76.1% (61.2% to 87.4%)     11
#>  75 and older        169        38 25/38 = 65.8% (48.6% to 80.4%)     13
#>                     false_alerts
#>  60/385 = 15.6% (12.1% to 19.6%)
#>  43/131 = 32.8% (24.9% to 41.6%)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sens_by_group <- tapply(test$alert[test$fracture == 1], test$age_group[test$fracture == 1], mean)
stopifnot(sens_by_group[["75 and older"]] < sens_by_group[["18 to 74"]])
```
:::


**Report.** At a threshold of 20%, the tool detects 35/46 = 76.1% (61.2% to 87.4%) of fractures in people aged 18 to
74 but only 25/38 = 65.8% (48.6% to 80.4%) in people aged 75 and older, and it raises false alerts for
43/131 = 32.8% (24.9% to 41.6%) of older people without a fracture. In this synthetic cohort, older patients
carry both more missed fractures and more unnecessary follow-up. The intervals overlap for sensitivity, so the
difference needs confirmation; the information missing to decide is the size and direction of this gap in real
local data.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reporting "sensitivity 71%" without the number of fractures behind it. With 38 fractures in a subgroup the 95%
interval spans more than 30 percentage points. Always give *x/n*.
:::

## Your record for the workshop

1. Two two-by-two tables (Part A) with all eight cells and both PPVs.
2. The results table (Part B) with the test denominator and a sentence on whether the extra effort is justified.
3. A threshold you would propose for the pilot, the group that is disadvantaged by it, and the one piece of
   information you would need before deciding (Part C).

Download the tables linked at the top if you want to continue in a spreadsheet. The script writes the same files
to `output/` when you run it on your own.
